questions.explanation: An LLM does one thing repeatedly: given some text, it predicts what probably comes next, adds that to the text, and predicts again. A whole essay is thousands of these tiny predictions strung together — like your phone's autocomplete, scaled up enormously. It isn't searching the web, following hand-written rules, or working like a human brain.

options.text: It searches the internet for the best answer to your question
It predicts the most likely next word, over and over, to build up a response
It follows a giant list of if-then rules written by programmers
It understands language the same way a human brain does

questions.prompt: At its core, what does a large language model actually do?

questions.explanation: There's no filing cabinet of facts inside. During training, the model absorbed patterns from a huge amount of text, and those patterns are stored in its internal dials. "Paris" comes out because it's overwhelmingly the most likely word to follow that question — more like remembering the gist of something you read than looking up an exact record. This is also why LLMs can confidently get facts wrong: likely-sounding is not the same as verified.

options.text: Yes — it has a fact database and finds the matching entry
Yes, but only for geography questions
No — its knowledge is baked into patterns from training, and it predicts "Paris" as the likely continuation
No — it asks a human operator behind the scenes

questions.prompt: When you ask an LLM "What is the capital of France?", does it look the answer up in a database of stored facts?

questions.explanation: It's the same fundamental move — predict the next word — but at a massively different scale. To predict really well, the model has to absorb facts, grammar, and patterns about how the world works, because finishing a sentence like "The capital of France is ___" quietly requires knowledge. That's why scale makes prediction feel like intelligence, without the model having beliefs of its own.

options.text: The LLM uses a completely different trick that has nothing to do with prediction
The LLM is connected to a team of experts who review its answers
Scale — it's trained on vastly more text with billions of internal dials, and very good prediction starts to look like understanding
The LLM genuinely understands and believes what it says, while your phone doesn't

questions.prompt: Your phone's autocomplete and an LLM both predict the next word. What's the main reason the LLM feels so much smarter?

questions.explanation: LLMs don't have beliefs, preferences, or plans — they produce text that plausibly continues what came before. Ask the same question framed a bit differently and the model might argue for the mountains instead. Remembering this helps you treat AI output as "likely text" to evaluate, rather than the testimony of someone with real opinions.

options.text: The model has genuinely reflected and formed a preference for beaches
The model produced a likely-sounding continuation of the conversation, not a real belief
The model's programmers hard-coded a pro-beach opinion into it
The model surveyed the internet in real time and beaches won

questions.prompt: An LLM writes: "I think the beach is the best vacation spot." What is the most accurate way to interpret this?

questions.explanation: The first three are the heart of the mental model: responses are generated piece by piece, the model weighs many possible continuations with different probabilities (remember the ambiguous round in the game?), and chat products wrap an LLM engine in an interface and safety training. The last two are false: the model only computes when given text to continue — it isn't thinking between messages — and it produces likely text, not verified text, which is why it can sound confident while being wrong.

options.text: A long response is built one small prediction at a time
For a given sentence start, several different next words can each be plausible
ChatGPT and Claude are products built around an LLM, like a car built around an engine
Between your messages, the model sits and thinks about what to say to you next
An LLM verifies every sentence against trusted sources before writing it

questions.prompt: Which of the following are TRUE about how LLMs work? (select all that apply)

questions.explanation: Before your text reaches the model, a tokenizer chops it into chunks called tokens — like a meal kit's pre-portioned packets. Common words like "the" or "coffee" get one token each; rare words are assembled from several smaller chunks. The model never sees letters or whole sentences directly — only this stream of tokens.

options.text: Individual letters, one at a time
Whole sentences as single units
Tokens — chunks of text that are sometimes whole words and sometimes pieces of words
A photograph of your screen

questions.prompt: What does an LLM actually "see" when it reads your message?

questions.explanation: The tokenizer has a fixed vocabulary of roughly a hundred thousand chunks, chosen by frequency. Anything that appears constantly in text (like "cat") gets its own short code, and anything rare gets spelled out from recognizable parts — like shorthand, where frequent phrases get their own symbol. Splits are based purely on frequency, not meaning, which is why your name may split in a spot that looks arbitrary.

options.text: Longer words are always split exactly every 4 letters, no exceptions
The tokenizer keeps a fixed menu of frequent chunks — common words earn their own token, rare words are assembled from smaller pieces
The model splits words it finds confusing or emotional
Scientific words are stored in a separate dictionary

questions.prompt: Why does a common word like "cat" become one token, while a rare word like "antidisestablishmentarianism" gets split into several?

questions.explanation: To the model, "strawberry" is a packet with a label, not a string of letters — asking it to count the r's is like asking someone to count grains of rice inside a sealed packet by reading the label. This is why LLMs are shaky at letter-level tasks in general: counting letters, reversing words, precise rhymes. The model reads at a different resolution than you do.

options.text: It never learned the alphabet during training
It sees "strawberry" as one or two sealed token chunks, not as ten individual letters
Spelling questions are blocked for safety reasons
It confuses strawberries with raspberries

questions.prompt: Why might an AI incorrectly count the number of r's in "strawberry"?

questions.explanation: The context window is the model's desk space, measured in tokens: everything it reads and writes in a conversation must fit within this budget. When a chat outgrows it, the oldest parts fall off the desk and the model genuinely can't see them anymore — which is why an AI can seem to "forget" the start of a long conversation. A later module explores this budget in depth.

options.text: The pop-up window where you type your message
The limit on how many tokens the model can handle in one conversation — its token budget
A tool that translates tokens back into words
The amount of time the model spends thinking before answering

questions.prompt: What is the "context window"?

questions.explanation: Pretraining is a flashcard game at colossal scale: hide the next word of real text, let the model guess, reveal the answer, and nudge the dials so the right word becomes slightly more likely next time. Repeated billions of times, this forces the dials to organize around grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns. Nothing is typed in by hand and nothing is stored as a searchable database — the knowledge lives in the dials as patterns.

options.text: Programmers typing millions of facts into the model by hand
Practicing next-word prediction on a giant library of text, billions of times, adjusting internal dials after each guess
Copying the whole internet into the model's database so it can look things up later
Humans chatting with the model until it learns to talk

questions.prompt: What is pretraining, in essence?

questions.explanation: The loop is guess, check, adjust — like flashcards. Each single round teaches almost nothing, but the tiny nudges accumulate across billions of examples. No human could correct guesses one by one at that scale (the "check" is automatic, because the real next word is right there in the text), and the model isn't memorizing documents or rewriting its code — only its dials change.

options.text: Guess the hidden word, check against the real text, adjust the internal dials slightly — then repeat billions of times
It memorizes each document word-for-word so it can recite it later
A human teacher corrects each individual guess by hand
It rewrites its own programming code whenever it makes a mistake

questions.prompt: During pretraining, how does the model actually improve at its guessing game?

questions.explanation: The raw model is like a brilliant actor with no role: it can imitate anyone in the library — helpful experts, trolls, spam bots — because likely continuation is its only goal. On the internet, a question is often followed by more questions, so that's a perfectly "correct" prediction! It has read plenty; what it lacks is a reason to be consistently helpful, honest, and safe. That's what phase two provides.

options.text: It's too slow to use until it gets optimized
It hasn't read enough text yet to answer questions
It only continues text in likely ways — it might answer your question with more questions, or imitate bad advice, because it learned from everything
It refuses to talk until it's given a personality

questions.prompt: Why isn't a freshly pretrained ("raw") model already a good assistant?

questions.explanation: Phase two has two main ingredients: finetuning (an apprenticeship on high-quality examples of the assistant job) and learning from human feedback, often called RLHF (reviewers rank answers, and the dials shift toward the kinds people rate as helpful and safe). Models are not retrained daily — training happens once and the dials freeze — and there's no built-in live database, which is exactly why knowledge cutoffs exist.

options.text: Finetuning on carefully chosen examples of helpful, honest conversations
Human reviewers ranking the model's answers — like thumbs up/down at scale — and nudging the dials toward highly rated ones
Retraining the model from scratch every morning on fresh data
Giving the model access to a live fact-checking database

questions.prompt: Which of these are part of turning a raw predictor into a helpful assistant? (select all that apply)

questions.explanation: The library the model learned from has a last page. Training happens once, on text gathered up to a certain date, and then the dials stop changing — so events after that date simply don't exist for the model. It isn't secrecy or forgetfulness. Practical takeaway: don't rely on a bare LLM for anything recent, and know that when products show current information, it's usually a bolted-on web search feeding the model, not the model's own knowledge.

options.text: Companies deliberately hide recent information for legal reasons
The model was trained on a snapshot of text collected up to a certain date, then its dials were frozen — nothing after that date exists for it
Old models get slower and forget the newest things they learned
Recent events are too controversial for the model to discuss

questions.prompt: Why does every LLM have a "knowledge cutoff" date?

exercise.instructions:
This is a two-step observation experiment.

Step 1 — Run the starter prompt as-is. It asks about a novel that does not exist ('The Glass Harbor' by Edwin Marsh, 1897 — we made it up). Read the response carefully. Does the model describe the plot, themes, or reception of a book that was never written? That's a hallucination, live in front of you.

Step 2 — Now edit the prompt to defuse it. Keep the same obscure question, but add explicit permission to admit uncertainty — for example: 'If you are not sure this book exists or are unsure about any detail, say so clearly — do not guess.' You can also ask it to separate what it actually knows from what it is unsure about. Run it again and compare the two responses.

Your score is based on your FINAL prompt: it should (1) ask about something specific and obscure enough to expose invention, (2) explicitly allow the model to say it doesn't know, and (3) ask it to distinguish what it knows from what it's unsure about.

rubric.description: The prompt asks about a specific, obscure, or fictional thing (e.g., a non-existent book, a very niche person or event) — something concrete and checkable that would expose invention if the model made up details.

The prompt explicitly gives the model permission to admit uncertainty or say it doesn't know, e.g., 'If you are not sure, say so — do not guess' or equivalent wording that makes 'I don't know' an acceptable answer.
The prompt asks the model to distinguish or separate what it actually knows from what it is unsure about (e.g., 'tell me which parts you are confident about and which you are not').

exercise.starterPrompt: Tell me about the 1897 novel 'The Glass Harbor' by Edwin Marsh. What is the plot, and how was it received by critics?
exercise.title: Watch a Hallucination Happen (Then Prevent It)

questions.explanation: An LLM generates the most plausible continuation of your text, word by word. Plausible is not the same as true — there is no built-in fact-checker verifying each claim, and no intent to deceive.

options.text: It is deliberately lying to keep the conversation going
It predicts plausible-sounding text from patterns — it doesn't look answers up in a database of verified facts
Its fact-checking module occasionally crashes
It only hallucinates when the user is rude to it

questions.prompt: Why does an LLM sometimes state false things with total confidence?

questions.explanation: Risk rises where training data is thin: obscure topics and very specific questions. The model fills the gaps with generic, plausible-shaped details. Famous, well-documented topics are much safer, and brainstorming has no 'wrong facts' to invent.

options.text: Asking for a summary of a world-famous, heavily documented event
Asking it to brainstorm names for a bakery
Asking a very specific factual question about an obscure topic it saw little training data on
Asking it to explain a common everyday concept

questions.prompt: In which situation is a hallucination MOST likely?

questions.explanation: Hallucinations are dangerous precisely because they're plausible: realistic fake citations, subtly wrong biographical details, and ballpark-but-wrong numbers. Absurd claims are rare — obviously silly text isn't a plausible continuation, so the model rarely produces it.

options.text: Beautifully formatted citations for papers that don't exist
A biography with a wrong birthplace or an award the person never won
Obviously absurd claims like 'the moon is made of soup'
Dates and statistics that are in the right ballpark but not real

questions.prompt: Which of these are classic hallucination traps to watch for? (Select all that apply.)

questions.explanation: Permission to admit uncertainty, self-critique follow-ups, and cross-checking all work. Confidence and detail are NOT signals of truth — hallucinated answers sound exactly as confident as correct ones.

options.text: Tell the model it's allowed to say 'I don't know' instead of guessing
Follow up with 'Are you sure? What might be wrong in that answer?'
Cross-check important facts against a second source
Trust the answer more when it sounds confident and detailed

questions.prompt: Which of these are effective everyday defenses against hallucination? (Select all that apply.)

questions.explanation: There's no internal 'I'm making this up' signal — correct and invented text are produced by the same pattern-prediction process. But prompting the model to express uncertainty ('say so if you're not sure') often surfaces the shaky parts, so your habits genuinely help.

options.text: Yes — it always knows, it just chooses not to tell you
Yes — an internal alarm fires whenever it invents something
Mostly no — invented answers are generated the same way as correct ones, so there's no built-in alarm; but explicitly asking it to flag uncertainty often helps
No — and there is nothing you can do about it

questions.prompt: Does the model know when its own answer is wrong?

exercise.instructions:
This is a two-step observation experiment.

Step 1 — Run the starter prompt. Then run it AGAIN, unchanged. Compare the two responses: different name? different slogan? different tone? That's the built-in randomness — the model rolled the dice differently each time.

Step 2 — Now edit the prompt to demand consistency. Constrain it hard: ask for exactly one name and one slogan, tell it to choose the most conventional/standard option (no creativity), and pin down the exact output format, e.g. 'Format: Name: ... / Slogan: ...'. Run your edited prompt twice and see how much more similar the two runs are.

Your score is based on your FINAL prompt: it should still be a creative-generation task (so variance is observable), explicitly ask for the single most standard/conventional answer, and explicitly constrain the output format.

rubric.description: The final prompt explicitly constrains the output format — e.g., specifies exactly one name and one slogan and a template like 'Name: ... / Slogan: ...' or an equally precise structure.
The prompt explicitly asks for the single most standard, conventional, or common answer (or tells the model not to be creative), which reduces run-to-run variance.
The prompt is a creative-generation task (naming, slogan, tagline, or similar open-ended invention) where run-to-run variance would be observable — not a pure factual lookup.

exercise.starterPrompt: Give me a name and one-line slogan for a coffee shop for night-owls.
exercise.title: Catch the Dice Roll (Then Tame It)

questions.explanation: Randomness is built in on purpose. The model computes probabilities for many candidate next words and samples among them; one different early pick reshapes everything after it. It's not retraining, memory, or a bug.

options.text: The model re-trains itself overnight and changes its opinions
At each word, the model rolls weighted dice over a menu of likely next words — different rolls send the answer down different paths
The model remembers your earlier question and deliberately avoids repeating itself
It's a bug that developers haven't fixed yet

questions.prompt: Why can the exact same question give different answers on different days?

questions.explanation: Temperature is a dial on the dice rolls: low means the top-probability word nearly always wins (predictable), high means lower-ranked words get picked more often (varied, sometimes weird). It doesn't affect speed, knowledge, or politeness.

options.text: How fast the model responds
How much the model knows about a topic
How adventurous the word choices are — low is predictable and repeatable, high is varied and creative
How polite the model's tone is

questions.prompt: What does the 'temperature' setting control?

questions.explanation: Facts and code have right answers — creativity only adds ways to be wrong, and you want the same input to give the same output. Brainstorming and creative writing are exactly where you WANT the dice to roll freely.

options.text: Answering a factual question
Brainstorming twenty possible podcast names
Generating code or precise step-by-step instructions
Writing a surprising opening line for a short story

questions.prompt: For which tasks is LOW randomness (high consistency) the better fit? (Select all that apply.)

questions.explanation: Your wording can do the dial's job: asking for the most standard/conventional option and pinning down the exact format makes the safe choice the plausible choice, so run-to-run variance shrinks. Capital letters change nothing, and re-rolling for a favorite is the opposite of repeatable.

options.text: Nothing — without the setting, consistency is impossible
Ask the same question many times and pick your favorite answer
Type the question in all capital letters to make it more serious
Ask in the prompt for 'the single most standard, conventional answer' and specify an exact output format

questions.prompt: You can't access any temperature setting in your chat app, but you need a consistent, repeatable answer. What's your best move?

questions.explanation: The model predicts likely next words. With a vague prompt, thousands of continuations are plausible, so you get the most average one. It isn't lazy (a) and prompt length doesn't change how much compute it gets (d) — the problem is that YOU haven't narrowed down what 'good' looks like.

options.text: The AI is being lazy and saving effort for harder questions
Many different continuations are equally likely, so the model lands on the statistical average
The AI doesn't know much about dogs
Short prompts are processed with less computing power

questions.prompt: Why does a vague prompt like "write about dogs" tend to produce a generic answer?

questions.explanation: Length, audience, the actual article, and emphasis are all real gaps — the model would have to guess each one. Politeness (d) is fine to include but doesn't change what the model produces; it's the one option that isn't a missing specification.

options.text: How long the summary should be
Who the summary is for
The article itself (or a clear pointer to it)
A polite greeting
What to emphasize or leave out

questions.prompt: Which of these are missing from the prompt "Summarize this article"? Select all that apply.

questions.explanation: Option c states the task (rewrite), audience (landlord), tone (firm but polite), a length limit, and includes the material. Urgency (a) and speed (b) add no specification, and a role alone (d) doesn't fix a vague task — roles help, but only on top of a clear request.

options.text: Please please help me with my email, it's really important
Help me write an email quickly
Rewrite this email to my landlord to sound firm but polite, under 150 words: [email text]
You are an email expert. Help me with my email.

questions.prompt: Which rewrite of "help me with my email" is most specific?

exercise.instructions: The starter prompt below is too vague: "give me a workout plan". Rewrite it into a specific prompt. Your prompt must (1) describe the person the plan is for (fitness level, and available time or equipment), (2) state a concrete goal, (3) set constraints on the plan itself (how many days per week, session length, or format), and (4) say anything to avoid or include (e.g. no gym, bad knees, must include stretching). Then run it and see how much better the answer gets.

rubric.description: The prompt describes who the plan is for: a fitness level plus available time and/or equipment.
The prompt states a concrete goal (e.g. run a 5k, build strength, lose weight, feel less stiff).

exercise.title: Sharpen a vague prompt

questions.explanation: The model only sees the text in front of it. It has no memory of you and no access to your life — like a brilliant stranger. It doesn't secretly know your situation (c), and extra words help only when they carry relevant facts, not effort (d).

options.text: It forgets everything between conversations and knows nothing about your situation unless you say it
It's a privacy feature you can turn off
It knows the facts but is required to ask anyway
Typing more words makes the model try harder

questions.prompt: Why does the model need you to spell out background facts it 'should' obviously need?

questions.explanation: A role steers prediction toward text that a person in that role would plausibly write — tone, depth, and framing. There's no hidden database (a) and no correctness guarantee (c): a confident teacher voice can still hallucinate. But roles measurably shape output, so (d) is wrong too.

options.text: Unlocks a hidden teacher database inside the model
Makes likely continuations sound like that role — its vocabulary, priorities, and way of explaining
Guarantees the answer is factually correct about chemistry
Nothing — roles are a superstition

questions.prompt: What does giving the model a role like "You are an experienced high-school chemistry teacher" actually do?

questions.explanation: The dispute, the actual message, and your desired outcome are the facts the reply depends on. A full life history (d) buries the question in text the model must wade through — include background only when the answer depends on it.

options.text: What the disagreement is about and how long it's been going on
The message she sent you
The outcome you want (e.g. make peace without giving in on the money)
Your full family history since childhood

questions.prompt: You're asking for help replying to a difficult message from your sister. Which details are worth including as context? Select all that apply.

exercise.instructions: Scenario: you want advice on asking your manager to work from home two days a week. Write a prompt that (1) assigns the model a relevant role (e.g. an experienced HR advisor or negotiation coach), (2) gives at least three pieces of background context — such as your job type, how long you've been there, your manager's known concerns, or a past precedent, (3) states the outcome you want, and (4) asks for a specific deliverable (e.g. talking points, or a short script for the conversation).

rubric.description: The prompt assigns the model a relevant role or persona.
The prompt includes at least three distinct pieces of background context about the situation.
The prompt states the desired outcome of the conversation with the manager.
The prompt requests a specific deliverable (talking points, script, email draft, etc.).

questions.explanation: Models continue patterns, so one concrete demonstration often beats a paragraph of description. Length alone doesn't help (b) — relevance does. The model follows the SHAPE of your example, not its words (c), and examples are optional, just powerful (d).

options.text: The model is a pattern continuer, so a demonstrated pattern strongly shapes what comes next
Examples make the prompt longer, and longer prompts always get better answers
The model copies your example word for word into the answer
Examples are required — the model errors without one

questions.prompt: Why is showing a small example of the format you want especially effective?

questions.explanation: Structure (a), length (c), and style (d) are the three format levers. "I'm choosing between three apartments" is context (b), and "compare them" is the task itself (e). Great prompts usually contain all three kinds.

options.text: "Answer in a table with columns Option / Cost / Risk"
"I'm choosing between three apartments"
"Keep it under 150 words"
"Use plain language a 12-year-old could follow"
"Compare the apartments for me"

questions.prompt: Which are format instructions (rather than task or context)? Select all that apply.

questions.explanation: Naming the structure (bulleted list), count (7), and length (one line each) removes the guesswork. Re-rolling the same prompt (a) just samples another essay-shaped answer; politeness (d) doesn't specify anything; and (c) — the model formats however you ask, once you actually ask.

options.text: Ask the exact same question again and hope for a shorter answer
Reask with explicit format: "Give me 7 dinner ideas as a bulleted list, one line each"
Give up — the model can only write essays
Add "please" to the original question

"That's wrong."

questions.explanation: The whole conversation so far is the model's working context, so "make the middle section shorter" is fully understandable. The model isn't getting smarter (a) — it just has more of your intent in view. Speed (c) is irrelevant to quality here.

options.text: The model gets smarter as the conversation goes on
Everything already said in the conversation is still in front of the model, so follow-ups build on it
Short messages are processed faster and more accurately
It can't — every message must repeat the full request

questions.prompt: Why can a follow-up message be much shorter than your first prompt?

questions.explanation: A long conversation full of wrong turns keeps steering predictions back toward those wrong turns. A fresh start with an upgraded prompt — specific, with context and format baked in — usually beats a fifth correction (a). The failure taught you the spec; use it.

options.text: Keep correcting — the fifth time is the charm
Start a fresh conversation with a new prompt that includes everything you learned to specify
Conclude the task is impossible for AI
Ask the model why it is being difficult

Imagine you asked for a short bio for your neighborhood book-club page and got this draft:

The message identifies at least two specific problems with the draft (naming words or qualities, not just 'make it better').
The message gives a concrete direction for the rewrite: a target tone, audience, or example phrasing.
The message states a desired length.

questions.explanation: The context window is the model's entire working view: your messages, its replies, and pasted documents, all in tokens. It's not permanent memory (a) — anything outside the window doesn't exist to the model — and it has nothing to do with time (c) or privacy (d).

options.text: The model's permanent memory of every conversation it has ever had
The finite amount of text — measured in tokens — the model can see at once
The time limit for the model to answer
A privacy screen that hides your data from the model

questions.prompt: What is the context window?

questions.explanation: Two mechanical causes: overflow (old text dropped from the window) or dilution (the instruction is still there but buried in so much text that attention over it is thin). No boredom, no rebellion — it's an attention budget being overspent.

options.text: The model got bored and stopped paying attention
The early messages scrolled out of the context window, or attention over the huge context got too thin
The model deleted the instruction because it disagreed with it
A software bug — this should never happen

questions.prompt: Your conversation has grown very long and the model no longer remembers an instruction from the start. What most likely happened?

questions.explanation: Trimming, positioning key asks at the edges, and fresh starts all concentrate attention on what matters. "Paste everything just in case" (c) is the classic budget-waster: every irrelevant token dilutes attention over the tokens you actually care about.

options.text: Trim a pasted document down to the relevant sections before sending it
Put your key instruction at the start or end, not buried in the middle
Paste in everything you have, just in case any of it helps
Start a fresh conversation when switching to an unrelated topic

questions.prompt: Which habits make good use of the attention budget? Select all that apply.

exercise.instructions: You have three paragraphs of meeting notes (invent them — a team meeting about planning a charity bake sale works fine) and ONE thing you need: the model must extract every date and deadline mentioned. Write a prompt that respects the attention budget: (1) state the extraction task clearly BEFORE the pasted notes, (2) include your invented notes (at least three short paragraphs, with 2–3 dates hidden inside), (3) after the notes, repeat the ask in one line, and (4) specify the output format (e.g. a bulleted list of 'date — what it's for').

questions.explanation: A model learns during training, from a fixed snapshot of text. Nothing after that snapshot exists in its learned knowledge. It's an engineering economics fact, not a paywall (a) or a legal rule (c) — and the model isn't forgetting (d); it never knew.

options.text: Companies hide recent knowledge behind a paywall
Training happens on a snapshot of text collected up to a date, and retraining is too expensive to do continuously
Recent events are legally off-limits for AI
The model forgets new information after a while

questions.prompt: Why do models have a knowledge cutoff at all?

questions.explanation: Prices, last night's results, and 'newest version' all depend on now — the model will either admit ignorance or, worse, guess fluently. Bread chemistry (b) and unit conversion (e) are stable knowledge that training covers well.

options.text: "What's the current price of this phone?"
"Why does bread rise?"
"Who won last night's game?"
"What's the newest version of this app and what changed?"
"How do I convert cups to milliliters?"

questions.prompt: Which questions are risky to ask a model WITHOUT giving it fresh information? Select all that apply.

questions.explanation: The context window is your door into the model's windowless room: it uses whatever you put in front of it, even things training never saw. It can't absorb news on its own (a) or remember harder (c) — but (d) is too pessimistic: supplied context works great.

options.text: Ask about it directly — models absorb news automatically
Paste the article into your prompt and ask your question about the pasted text
Ask the model to try really hard to remember
It's impossible for a model to discuss anything after its cutoff

questions.prompt: You need the model's help interpreting a news story from last week. What's the reliable approach?

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis explanations appear countless times in training text — prediction alone nails it. The other three require constructing an answer specific to your inputs (arithmetic, constraint-juggling, counting), which is reasoning, where step-by-step errors creep in.

options.text: Computing the total cost of 17 items with different prices and a 12% discount
Explaining what photosynthesis is
Working out a fair chore schedule for 5 roommates with conflicting constraints
Counting how many times the letter 'e' appears in a paragraph

questions.prompt: Which task relies mostly on RECALL?

questions.explanation: Your particular numbers never appeared in training, so prediction can't just retrieve the answer — it must derive it, and every intermediate step is a chance for error. Math is well represented in training (a); this is about construction vs retrieval, not difficulty of the subject (d).

options.text: Math was excluded from the training data
The specific answer isn't in training text — it must be constructed step by step, and each step can slip
Models dislike numbers
Historical facts are simpler than all math

questions.prompt: Why are multi-step math problems harder for a next-word predictor than famous historical facts?

questions.explanation: Wrong totals are the signature of reasoning slips. Asking for step-by-step work both improves accuracy and lets YOU spot exactly where it slipped. It's not a missing fact (a) or stale knowledge (c), and rerunning blind (d) leaves you unable to tell a right answer from a lucky-looking wrong one.

options.text: A recall failure — provide the correct fact in your prompt
A reasoning failure — ask it to show its work step by step and check the steps
A knowledge-cutoff problem — paste in a newer article
Random bad luck — just rerun until the total looks right

questions.prompt: The model gives you a wrong total in a budget calculation. What kind of failure is this, and what helps?

exercise.instructions: Give the model a small reasoning problem and force step-by-step work. rubric.description: The prompt contains a concrete multi-step problem with specific numbers.
The prompt explicitly requests step-by-step working with intermediate calculations shown.
The prompt asks for the final answer on a clearly labeled final line.

exercise.title: Make it show its work

questions.explanation: Training text — articles, textbooks, explanations — overwhelmingly sounds sure of itself, so confident tone is simply the likeliest style to predict. Tone is part of the output, not a self-report of certainty. There's no deception motive (a) and no reliable hesitancy signal (d).

options.text: The model is trained to deceive users
Confident phrasing is the most likely continuation style in its training text, produced the same way whether the fact is right or invented
The model is always at least 90% sure of what it says
Wrong answers actually do sound noticeably more hesitant

questions.prompt: Why do wrong answers from an LLM usually sound just as confident as right ones?

questions.explanation: Dosages and filing deadlines are high-stakes (and for medical questions, AI should only assist a professional or primary source, never replace one); a statistic you'll repeat publicly is medium-stakes and worth checking. Brainstormed names (b) and a poem (e) are low-stakes — usefulness is the only test, so verification adds nothing.

options.text: It suggested a medication dosage for your child
It brainstormed 20 names for your book club
It stated a statistic you're about to put in a presentation
It gave you a deadline for a government form you must file
It drafted a silly birthday poem

questions.prompt: Which situations call for verifying the model's answer before acting on it? Select all that apply.

questions.explanation: Contradiction under reruns is a hallucination red flag: the model is sampling plausible-sounding answers, not retrieving a solid fact. Order (a), averaging (c), and length or detail (d) carry no evidence — detail is generated as fluently as everything else. Go to a primary source.

options.text: The first answer is right because it came first
At least one confident answer is wrong — treat the fact as unverified and check a real source
Average the two answers
The longer, more detailed answer is the correct one

questions.prompt: You ask the same factual question in two fresh conversations and get confident but CONTRADICTORY answers. What should you conclude?

questions.explanation: Stakes-based checking is the working professional's approach: it keeps the speed benefits for low-stakes work while protecting you where errors are costly. Blanket trust (a) ignores everything this lesson showed; blanket verification (b) or only-known-answers (d) throws away most of the tool's value.

options.text: Trust everything from the model that sounds professional
Verify every single output no matter how trivial, or don't use AI at all
Match your checking effort to the stakes: use drafts freely, verify facts you'll rely on, and keep AI as assistant-only for medical, legal, and financial decisions
Only use AI for questions you already know the answer to

questions.prompt: Which is the best use of the 'trust / verify / wrong-tool' rule?

questions.explanation: A demonstrated input→output pattern is the strongest possible signal to a next-word predictor: continuing the pattern is the most likely thing to do. Descriptions still work (c is wrong), length alone is irrelevant (a), and randomness isn't disabled (d) — it's just channeled.

options.text: Examples make the prompt longer, and longer is better
The model is a pattern continuer — a demonstrated pattern constrains the output more tightly than a description
Descriptions are ignored by the model
Examples turn off the model's randomness

questions.prompt: Why do a few worked examples often beat a paragraph describing what you want?

questions.explanation: Inconsistent formats blur the pattern, identical examples teach nothing about range, and the model faithfully copies flaws — it can't tell your mistakes from your intentions. Two or three GOOD examples (d) is not a mistake; it's usually the sweet spot.

options.text: Examples that each use a slightly different format
Examples that are all nearly identical, covering no variety
An example containing the exact sloppy habit you don't want copied
Using only two or three examples instead of ten

questions.prompt: Which are real few-shot mistakes to avoid? Select all that apply.

questions.explanation: Tone is exactly what examples teach best — 'warm' means something specific once it's demonstrated twice. Shouting an adjective (a) or asking for imagination (c) leaves 'warm' undefined, and rerolling (d) is gambling, not prompting.

options.text: Add "be warm!" in capital letters
Include two example reviews each followed by the kind of warm, short reply you want, then the new review
Ask the model to imagine being warm before answering
Rerun the prompt until a warm one appears

questions.prompt: You want short, warm replies to customer reviews, but the model keeps writing stiff corporate ones. Which fix uses few-shot prompting?

exercise.instructions: Create a few-shot prompt that turns plain product review text into a one-line label of the form 'MOOD — five-word summary' (e.g. 'HAPPY — loves the battery life'). Keep instructions minimal — let the examples do the teaching.

rubric.description: The prompt contains at least two complete input→output example pairs.
All examples use the same output format ('MOOD — short summary').
At least one example covers a negative or mixed review.
The prompt ends with a new unlabeled review for the model to label.

questions.explanation: Tags are labeled envelopes: the model treats them as strong section boundaries, so it stops rewriting your instructions when you meant it to rewrite your email. They're optional (c), have no speed effect (a), and hide nothing (d).

options.text: They make the prompt run faster
They mark clear boundaries so the model can't confuse your instructions with the material you pasted in
They are required syntax — untagged prompts are rejected
They encrypt sensitive sections

questions.prompt: What problem do XML tags solve in a prompt?

questions.explanation: Option b labels each section by its content, closes every tag, and cross-references the <email> section by name from the instructions. (a) puts the instruction in the email envelope, (c) never closes the envelope, and (d) is noise — tag SECTIONS, not sentences.

options.text: <email>Rewrite this politely</email> followed by the pasted email with no tag
<instructions>Rewrite the text in <email> to be politer.</instructions> then <email>...pasted email...</email>
<email>...pasted email... (no closing tag, instructions mixed inside)
Wrapping every individual sentence of the prompt in its own tag

questions.prompt: Which prompt uses tags correctly?

questions.explanation: Three kinds of content, three labeled envelopes. One tag around everything (c) draws no boundaries at all. And while tags don't have reserved names, DESCRIPTIVE names (b) beat meaningless ones (d) — the name itself tells the model what the section is.

options.text: No tags — short prompts don't need them
<instructions>, <notes> for the pasted notes, and <examples> containing the two samples
One giant <everything> tag around the whole prompt
<a>, <b>, <c> — the names don't matter

questions.prompt: You're asking for a summary of meeting notes and also including two example summaries you like. What's the best tag layout?

exercise.instructions: You need the model to turn rough interview notes into three polished FAQ entries. Write a prompt with clear XML structure: (1) an <instructions> section stating the task and the output format (question line + 2–3 sentence answer), (2) a <notes> section containing invented rough notes (5+ lines of fragmented notes about, say, a community garden's rules), (3) an <example> section with ONE example FAQ entry in your desired format, and (4) inside <instructions>, refer to the other sections by their tag names (e.g. 'using the material in <notes>, matching the format shown in <example>'). Every tag must be properly opened and closed.

rubric.description: The prompt contains distinct <instructions>, <notes>, and <example> tagged sections, all properly opened and closed.

The instructions refer to at least one other section by its tag name.

exercise.title: Tag a messy prompt

questions.explanation: The model writes one token at a time and can only lean on visible text. Steps are stepping stones: each conclusion rests on written work rather than a blind leap. There's no hidden timer (a) or math mode (c), and length only helps when it's load-bearing reasoning (d).

options.text: It gives the model more time to think in the background
Each token builds on what's already written, so written intermediate steps give the final answer solid support
It activates a special math mode
Longer answers are always more accurate

questions.prompt: Why does asking for step-by-step reasoning improve accuracy on multi-step problems?

questions.explanation: Visible steps are auditable: instead of 'that's wrong, try again', you can say 'step 3 double-counts the discount — redo from there', which is exactly the targeted iteration you learned in module 02. Steps reduce some errors but certify nothing (b, c), and they make responses longer, not shorter (d).

options.text: You can find the exact step that went wrong and correct it surgically
The answer becomes legally certified
It prevents all hallucination
It makes the response shorter

questions.prompt: Besides accuracy, what's the second big benefit of visible reasoning steps?

questions.explanation: Multi-factor comparisons, arithmetic, and constraint juggling are construction tasks — steps carry real weight. A haiku (b) needs no derivation, and a treaty date (d) is pure recall: the model either knows it or hallucinates it, and steps won't change which.

options.text: Comparing two job offers across salary, commute, and growth
Writing a haiku about autumn
Working out whether a monthly budget balances
Recalling what year a famous treaty was signed
Scheduling three activities around fixed constraints

questions.explanation: Machines and downstream steps need predictable shapes; a friendly 'Sure! Here's...' wrapper breaks them. For a human skim (a), prose is fine — strictness is a tool for reuse, not a universal rule (c). And JSON is just labeled text anyone can read (d).

options.text: When a human will casually read the answer once
When something other than a human — a spreadsheet, app, or your next prompt — will consume the output
Always — prose answers are wrong
Never — JSON is only for programmers

questions.prompt: When does forcing output into strict JSON matter most?

questions.explanation: Named fields, a demonstrated example, the only-the-JSON sentence, and an unknowns rule are the four pillars — the last one is your hallucination guard. Commentary after the JSON (d) is exactly the wrapper text you're trying to eliminate.

options.text: The exact field names and what type each holds
One example object in the desired shape
An instruction to respond with ONLY the JSON, no extra text
An instruction to add helpful commentary after the JSON
A rule for unknown values (e.g. use null, don't invent)

questions.prompt: Which elements belong in a reliable JSON-constraining prompt? Select all that apply.

questions.explanation: Shape and truth are independent: the model fills required fields with the most plausible-looking values, real or not. Format validity verifies nothing (a, c), and it only uses null for unknowns if you TOLD it to — and even then, verify anything load-bearing (d).

options.text: Valid JSON format means the contents were verified
Formatting constrains the shape, not the truth — the content can still be hallucinated
JSON output disables hallucination
The model would have used null if it weren't sure

rubric.description: The prompt names the exact fields (name, minutes, difficulty, ingredients) with their types or allowed values.

questions.explanation: The system prompt is the employee handbook: identity, standing rules, and conventions set before any user message arrives. Your first typed message is still a user prompt (a) — the system prompt was already there, usually invisible to you.

options.text: The first message you type in any conversation
Standing instructions given to the model before the conversation starts, shaping how it handles every message
An error message from the operating system
A prompt written by another AI

"Always give metric measurements alongside imperial ones"
"Here's tonight's fridge contents: eggs, spinach, rice"
"Never suggest recipes containing peanuts"
"Make this one vegetarian"

options.text: The model was specially trained only on that bank's documents
The app's system prompt sets those standing rules for every conversation
Coincidence — the model just tends to act that way
Users voted on the personality

options.text: Claude Code uses a smarter model

Claude Code can't hold a conversation
Chat assistants can't write code

questions.explanation: Observe is the step that makes it an agent: the actual output of the command flows back into the loop, so mistakes get caught and corrected. It doesn't declare victory blind (b) or need you to relay results (d) — seeing outcomes for itself is the whole point.

options.text: It observes the result of that action and uses it to decide what to do next

It waits for you to describe what happened

Prompts only matter for the first message

Because it takes real actions on real files — consequences require consent
Because the model is malicious by default
It's a legal formality with no practical effect

Close the terminal and start over

Extended thinking happens privately before the answer, letting the model explore and self-correct; written steps appear in the reply for YOU to audit
Extended thinking is only for math problems
Written steps are always better because they're visible

questions.prompt: How does extended thinking differ from asking for step-by-step reasoning in the reply?

questions.explanation: The budget is the whiteboard hour: more room to try approaches, catch mistakes, and reconsider — valuable exactly when the problem is hard, and paid for in wait time and compute. options.text: It buys more exploration and self-correction on hard problems; it costs time and money
It buys access to newer training data; it costs nothing

questions.prompt: What does a bigger thinking budget buy, and what does it cost?

questions.explanation: Multi-constraint comparisons, scheduling puzzles, and hunt-the-error tasks reward exploration and self-checking — whiteboard work. A capital city (b) is instant recall and a one-sentence rewrite (d) is hallway-level; deep thinking there just adds waiting.

options.text: Comparing two apartment leases with different fees, terms, and break clauses
What's the capital of France?
Planning a conference schedule where speakers have overlapping availability
Rewriting one sentence to sound friendlier
Finding the flaw in a budget that somehow doesn't balance

Your job, which is very important to our business, is to carefully read the customer's message and classify it appropriately. Please make sure to read the entire message carefully before deciding. Please remember that it is very important to choose only one of these four categories, and please do not invent new categories, because our system only understands these four categories and will break otherwise. Once you have carefully chosen the category, please also write a short reply to the customer. The reply should be brief — ideally just one sentence — and should acknowledge their concern in a friendly and professional manner. Please be very careful never to promise a refund in your reply, as only human agents are authorized to approve refunds, and promising one would create serious problems for our support team. Speaking of formatting, please output your answer in exactly this format: the first line should say 'category:' followed by the category, and the second line should say 'reply:' followed by your reply. Please do not add any other text, explanations, or formatting, as our automated system parses your output. One more thing: sometimes customers write in languages other than English. If the message is not in English, please classify it as other, but please still write your one-sentence reply in English. Thank you so much for your careful attention to all of these details! The customer's message will be provided between triple quotes below. Please handle it according to all of the instructions above.
